newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea sees 5.1 percent growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea sees 5.1 percent growth in 1997.

text.p: Papua New Guinea was expected to achieve 5.1 percent economic growth in calendar 1997 after moving out of recession last year, the governor of the South Pacific nation's central bank said.

Bank of Papua New Guinea governor Koiari Tarata, speaking after the bank issued the December 1996 quarterly bulletin, said the country achieved real gross domestic product of 1.9 percent in 1996 following a 2.9 percent decline in 1995.

"What we have witnessed so far will continue through 1997 with the growth a bit more pronounced, rising by 5.1 percent," he said, citing growth in the agriculture sector as the mainstay of the recovery.

He said the 1996 growth rate was mainly achieved due to strong growth in agriculture, which is dominated by coffee, cocoa and coconut production, as well as a recovery in the construction sector which was boosted by work on the A$700 billion Lihir gold mine.
The 14.6 million ounce mine is due to begin ore processing next month.
The island nation's commerce and manufacturing sectors had also achieved growth in 1996, after taking inflation into account.
Tatara forecast that with agricultural exports, with the exception of coffee, would improve in 1997.

He said that the economic recovery in 1996 was highlighted by a sharp rise in employment levels, a lower inflation rate due to prudent fiscal and monetary policies over the past two years, a return to surplus in the government's fiscal operations, and higher revenue led by a sharp rise in tax receipts.
However, the recovery was accompanied by rising general and mining sector imports, with the 1996 trade surplus falling to 1.331 billion kina from 1.800 billion kina in 1995.
Tarata said a fall in the value of gold and copper exports contributed to the lower trade surplus.
